title: YOU'RE ENGAGED, NOT MARRIED… SO IS SEXTING STILL A SIN IN GOD'S EYES?
paragraphs: YOU'RE ENGAGED, NOT MARRIED… SO IS SEXTING STILL A SIN IN GOD'S EYES?

You have the ring. You've made the promise. You're planning a future together. But does being almost married give you permission to awaken desires God intended for marriage? The answer may challenge your relationship, expose a dangerous misunderstanding about love, and reveal something beautiful about the grace of Jesus Christ.
There's a conversation happening behind closed doors that many Christians are too embarrassed to bring into the light.
It usually begins innocently.
A goodnight message.
An affectionate compliment.
An "I wish you were here."

Then the conversation becomes more intimate. The words become suggestive. Pictures are exchanged. Desires are described. And suddenly, two people who genuinely love Jesus find themselves doing things through a phone that they would be uncomfortable doing in front of their pastor.
But there's a question they keep asking themselves.
"We're getting married anyway… so is it really a sin?"
After all, they're not strangers.
They're not casually dating.

They've prayed together. They've talked about their future. They've chosen each other. They've bought the ring, perhaps booked the venue, and already imagined the day they'll stand before God and exchange their vows.
Surely that commitment must count for something.
And it does.
But here is the question that changes everything:
Does a promise to enter marriage give us permission to enjoy the sexual privileges of marriage before the covenant has actually begun?
Before you answer, stay with me.
Because this isn't simply an article about inappropriate messages, sexual temptation, or what Christians should and shouldn't do.
It's about something much deeper.
It's about the difference between loving someone and consuming someone.
Between intimacy and imitation intimacy.
Between the excitement of being wanted and the holiness of being loved.
And ultimately, it's about a Savior who does not expose our sin to humiliate us, but calls us out of darkness because He loves us too much to leave us there.
Perhaps you're reading this because you've already crossed a line.
Perhaps you've exchanged pictures you now regret.
Perhaps you've justified conversations that troubled your conscience.
Or perhaps you're engaged to someone you genuinely love, and you're desperately trying to understand how to honor God while experiencing desires that feel almost impossible to control.
If that's you, don't close this article.
There is truth here that may confront you.
But there is grace here, too.
And you need both.
Because the same Jesus who calls you to purity is the Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners into His arms.
Let's begin with something that might surprise you.
The Bible never uses the word "sexting."
Not once.
There were no smartphones in ancient Israel. No disappearing messages in Corinth. No private video calls in Ephesus.
So we must be careful not to pretend that Scripture directly addresses a technology that did not exist when it was written.
But Scripture does address the human heart.
It addresses lust, sexual conduct, self-control, covenant faithfulness, and the way we treat another person's body.
And those truths are not made irrelevant by a glowing screen.
Jesus said something in Matthew 5:27–28 that should make every believer examine the motives behind their private conversations:
"You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (ESV)
The Greek expression translated "with lustful intent" includes the phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).
It communicates looking at someone for the purpose of lusting after that person.
The verb epithymeō means to desire or long for something. The word itself is not always sinful in Scripture. Context determines whether the desire is appropriate or disordered.
And that distinction matters.
Jesus was not teaching that every experience of attraction is adultery.
He was confronting the deliberate cultivation of wrongful sexual desire.
He was exposing the heart that treats another person as an object of sexual gratification.
His immediate example concerns a man looking lustfully at a woman, but His teaching reveals a broader moral principle: outward restraint alone does not make the heart pure.
Now think about that in the context of sexting.
When two unmarried people intentionally exchange sexually explicit messages, images, or descriptions to arouse one another, they are not merely communicating affection.
They are deliberately cultivating sexual excitement outside the marriage covenant.

And while Christians may disagree about the boundaries of some romantic expressions, sexually explicit sexting designed to produce sexual arousal before marriage is difficult to reconcile with Jesus' teaching on purity and the New Testament's call to sexual holiness.
That is not a judgment on the sincerity of your love.
It is a challenge to what you believe love permits.
Because love can be genuine while a particular behavior is still wrong.
You can sincerely want to marry someone and still need to repent of how you have treated them.
You can deeply care about a person's future while making decisions that compromise your shared obedience to Christ.
And you can have a ring on your finger while still needing boundaries around your heart.
This brings us to one of the most misunderstood realities of Christian engagement.
An engagement is a promise of marriage. It is not marriage itself.

In biblical times, betrothal was often more legally binding than modern engagement. Matthew 1:18–19 describes Mary as betrothed to Joseph, while also explaining that they had not yet come together. Joseph is even described as considering divorce when he initially misunderstood Mary's pregnancy.
The historical arrangements were different from many modern engagements.
Yet the distinction remains important.
A binding commitment to marry did not mean that every aspect of married life had already begun.
The Hebrew Scriptures describe marital union with the expression בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad), meaning "one flesh," in Genesis 2:24.
The verse describes a man leaving his father and mother, holding fast to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
Jesus later affirmed this passage in Matthew 19:4–6 when teaching about marriage.
Biblically, marriage is not simply the presence of strong feelings or the certainty of future plans.
It is a covenantal union.
And sexual intimacy belongs within that union.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
"Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous." (ESV)
Notice what Scripture honors.
Marriage.
Not merely the intention to marry.
Not the certainty that the wedding will happen.
Not the emotional intensity of a relationship.
Marriage itself.
That distinction is not designed to punish engaged couples.
It is designed to protect the meaning of the covenant they are preparing to enter.
Imagine being invited to a beautiful wedding reception.
The tables are prepared. The candles are glowing. The food is waiting. Everything has been arranged for a celebration.
But the ceremony has not yet happened.
Would the beauty of the preparations make the covenant unnecessary?
Of course not.
The preparations are meaningful precisely because they point toward something that has not yet taken place.
In a similar way, engagement is a season of preparation.
It is not permission to treat the future as though it has already arrived.
And this is where many couples begin bargaining with their consciences.
"We're not actually having sex."
"It's only words."
"We're not touching each other."
"It's private."
"We already belong to each other."
But consider this.
If the purpose of the messages is to create sexual arousal, does the absence of physical touch automatically make the interaction spiritually harmless?
The New Testament does not reduce sexual holiness to avoiding one particular physical act.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5:
The Greek word translated "sexual immorality" is πορνεία (porneia).
In New Testament usage, it is a broad term for sexually immoral conduct. It should not be treated as a technical Greek word that directly names every modern behavior, including sexting.
But the passage gives us more than a category of prohibited acts.
It gives us a vision of sexual integrity.
Holiness.
Honor.
Self-control.
And the refusal to be governed by lust.
Paul's concern is not simply whether someone has found a technical loophole.
His concern is whether a believer's conduct reflects belonging to God.
So perhaps the better question is not:
"How far can we go without technically having sex?"
Perhaps the better question is:
"How can we love each other in a way that makes obedience to Jesus easier rather than harder?"
That question changes the atmosphere of a relationship.
It replaces loopholes with love.
It replaces pressure with protection.
It replaces the fear of missing out with the joy of honoring God together.
And it exposes another uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes what we call intimacy is actually a demand for access.
"Send me something."
"Prove you want me."
"If you really love me, you wouldn't be so hesitant."
"We're going to be married anyway."
Those words can sound playful in the beginning.
But when one person feels pressured to send intimate pictures or participate in explicit conversations against their conscience, something deeply troubling has entered the relationship.
Love does not require someone to violate their convictions to prove their devotion.
Love does not punish someone for saying no.
Love does not turn engagement into an entitlement to another person's body.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 13:5 that love "does not insist on its own way" (ESV).
That principle matters in every stage of a relationship, including marriage.
Your fiancé or fiancée is not an object you are waiting to possess.
They are a human being made in God's image.
A person whose dignity matters before the wedding and after it.
A person whose spiritual well-being should matter more to you than your immediate gratification.
And if you truly intend to spend the rest of your life with someone, learning to honor their boundaries now is not a burden.
It is preparation for faithful love.
There is another danger we cannot ignore.
Digital intimacy leaves digital traces.
A private photograph can be saved, copied, forwarded, stolen, or exposed through a compromised account.
A relationship can change.
An engagement can end.
A device can be lost.
Even when both people trust each other completely, technology introduces risks that neither person fully controls.
This does not mean that everyone who has shared intimate images will experience betrayal or exposure.
It means that wisdom should consider consequences beyond the moment.
And it means that if someone has already shared intimate material, they deserve practical help, not humiliation.

If you and your fiancé have crossed these boundaries, you may need to stop exchanging explicit material, discuss deleting existing copies, secure your accounts, and establish clear expectations about privacy.
If someone threatens to distribute intimate images, that is abuse, not an ordinary relationship disagreement. Seek trusted support and appropriate legal assistance.
And if either person is under eighteen, intimate images can create serious safeguarding and legal concerns even when they were exchanged voluntarily.
Purity should never be used as an excuse to shame victims, conceal coercion, or avoid protecting vulnerable people.
The God who calls us to holiness also commands us to act with justice, mercy, and love.
But now we come to the part that may be hardest to hear.
What if both people consent?
What if neither feels pressured?
What if the relationship is loving, respectful, and genuinely headed toward marriage?
Does that make sexually explicit sexting acceptable?
Consent is essential to ethical conduct, but consent alone does not settle every question of Christian morality.
Two people can willingly participate in something and still need to ask whether it honors God.
Christian discipleship does not teach that every mutually desired act is therefore righteous.
It teaches that our desires, choices, and relationships belong under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:20:
"For you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body." (ESV)
The context concerns sexual immorality and the believer's union with Christ.
Paul is not discussing mobile phones.
But the principle reaches beyond first-century technology.
Your body belongs to God.
Your sexuality matters to God.
And the ways you invite another person into sexual desire are not spiritually insignificant simply because they happen through a screen.
Yet there is a distinction we must preserve.
Not every affectionate message between engaged Christians is sexting.
Telling your fiancé that you find them beautiful is not automatically lust.
Expressing excitement about your future marriage is not inherently sinful.
Talking respectfully about sexual expectations, marital intimacy, concerns, boundaries, or questions before the wedding can be healthy and wise.
Even acknowledging sexual attraction does not mean you have already sinned.
The issue is not whether two engaged people experience desire.
The issue is what they choose to do with it.
There is a meaningful difference between discussing sex thoughtfully in preparation for marriage and deliberately using explicit exchanges to stimulate sexual gratification outside marriage.
Christian purity is not the denial that sexuality exists.
It is the ordering of sexuality according to God's purposes.
And that brings us to a sentence some people desperately need to hear:
Being tempted does not mean you have already failed God.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Temptation and sin are not identical.
Experiencing attraction is not the same as deliberately nurturing lust.
Having a sexual desire is not the same as deciding that desire should rule you.
The Christian life is not about becoming a person who never experiences temptation.
It is about learning, by God's grace, to respond to temptation with faithfulness.
But what happens when you don't?
What happens when you have already sent the pictures?
When you have already crossed the boundaries?
When you've said, "This is the last time," only to repeat the same behavior?
When you love Jesus but feel like a hypocrite every time you open your Bible?
When you wonder whether your future marriage has already been stained by the choices you've made?
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
Because if the Christian message were only "Be pure," every sinner would eventually run out of hope.
But the Gospel says something far more extraordinary.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not people with harmless pasts.
Real sinners.
People with hidden histories.
People who have broken promises.
People who have pursued pleasure without wisdom.
People who knew better and did it anyway.
People who feel ashamed of what they have done.
And people who have become so accustomed to compromise that they barely feel conviction anymore.
In John 8:1–11, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.

The scene is complicated by questions about the passage's textual history. The account is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John, so it should not be treated as our only foundation for doctrine.
Nevertheless, the story, as preserved in the Christian tradition, presents a striking picture of mercy and moral seriousness.
Jesus refuses to join the crowd in condemning the woman.
Yet He also tells her to leave her life of sin.
Mercy does not become permission.
And holiness does not become cruelty.
That balance is central to the message of Christ.
The clearest foundation for forgiveness is not dependent on that one disputed passage.
It runs throughout the New Testament.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (ESV)
Read that again.
Not some unrighteousness.
Not only the mistakes you made before you knew better.
All unrighteousness.
Forgiveness is not earned by pretending the sin was harmless.
It is received through the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
And repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and direction.
Biblically, repentance is a turning toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
It is not simply saying, "I'm sorry," while carefully preserving every opportunity to repeat the same sin.
It means being willing to change.
To establish boundaries.
To admit what has been wrong.
To ask for help.
To stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
And when you fall, to return to Christ rather than surrender to despair.
Perhaps you and your fiancé need a conversation that begins with something like this:

"I love you. I want to marry you. I am attracted to you. But I don't want us to build our future by repeatedly crossing boundaries that trouble our conscience. I want us to honor Jesus together, even when that means waiting."
Imagine hearing that from someone who genuinely loves you.
Not rejection.
Not coldness.
Not a declaration that you are undesirable.
But a promise that your spiritual good matters more than a temporary moment of excitement.
That is not the absence of passion.
It is passion learning patience.
And patience is not a meaningless inconvenience.
It is one of the ways love becomes trustworthy.
Galatians 5:22–23 identifies self-control as part of the fruit of the Spirit.
The Greek word ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia) refers to self-control or mastery over one's impulses.
It does not mean that Christians become emotionless.
It means that desire no longer has to be the master.
And what a beautiful foundation that can become for marriage.
Because marriage itself will require self-control.
There will be seasons of exhaustion.
Times of illness.
Periods of separation.
Emotional struggles.
Moments when one spouse desires intimacy and the other does not.
Marriage does not eliminate the need for patience, mutual respect, tenderness, or consent.
So the ability to hear "not now" without resentment is not merely useful during engagement.
It is a gift to your future spouse.
And the ability to say "I love you enough to wait" can become an expression of mature affection.
But I want to speak to another person now.
The one who is afraid to tell their fiancé that the sexting needs to stop.
Perhaps every attempt to establish boundaries turns into an argument.
Perhaps they accuse you of being judgmental.
Perhaps they tell you that refusing means you don't trust them.
Perhaps they threaten to leave.
Please understand this.
A wedding date is not a reason to ignore coercion.
If your fiancé refuses to respect your sexual boundaries, that is a serious concern worth addressing before marriage.
Seek counsel from a trustworthy pastor, qualified counselor, or mature Christian mentor who understands both biblical teaching and healthy relationship dynamics.
If there is intimidation, manipulation, or abuse, prioritize your safety and seek appropriate support.
You do not owe anyone sexual access because you accepted a proposal.
Not even someone you deeply love.
And not even someone you fully intend to marry.
A healthy engagement should make room for honest conversations, mutual respect, and genuine freedom to say no.
Now perhaps you're thinking:
"Does this mean we need to break up because we've sexted?"
Not necessarily.
Past sin does not automatically mean a relationship is beyond repair.
A couple can acknowledge wrongdoing, repent, rebuild trust, and establish healthier boundaries.
But neither should they rush into marriage simply to escape temptation.
Paul does discuss marriage in relation to sexual desire in 1 Corinthians 7:8–9, but that passage is not permission to enter a lifelong covenant impulsively or ignore serious relationship problems.
Marriage should be entered with wisdom, readiness, mutual commitment, and sober understanding of its responsibilities.
A wedding does not magically heal dishonesty, manipulation, compulsive behavior, or spiritual immaturity.
Those issues deserve attention before the vows.
And if you've already fallen into sexual compromise, you do not need to pretend everything is fine.
You can begin again with honesty.
Perhaps that means agreeing not to send explicit images.
Perhaps it means avoiding conversations that repeatedly escalate into sexual arousal.
Perhaps it means changing the time or setting of your late-night calls.
Perhaps it means inviting wise accountability from someone who will help without humiliating you.
Perhaps it means seeking professional support when sexual behavior feels compulsive or is connected to trauma.
Boundaries will look different across couples, but the goal should remain the same.
Not merely to avoid being caught.
Not to perform holiness for other Christians.
Not to prove that you are spiritually superior.
But to honor Jesus Christ with the relationship you have entrusted to Him.
And please remember this:
Your wedding night is not a reward God gives you for achieving perfect purity.
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not a prize for people who never struggled.
It is part of God's good design for marital union.
If you have a sexual past, you are not permanently disqualified from a faithful, loving marriage.
If you have sexted, you are not ruined.
If you have sinned sexually, your identity does not have to remain chained to that sin.
First Corinthians 6:11 speaks to believers who had formerly lived in various sins:
"And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God." (ESV)
"And such were some of you."
There is a world of hope in those words.
Paul does not deny the reality of their past.
He announces that their past no longer has the final word over who they are in Christ.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because they became impressive enough to deserve salvation.
But because of Jesus Christ.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who bore sin on the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and gives them a new life.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
We are not saved by sexual purity.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Grace does not tell us that sin is harmless.
Grace tells us that sin does not have to remain our master.
Maybe that is what you need to hear today.
Not another voice telling you that you are disgusting.
Not another excuse telling you that nothing needs to change.
But the voice of Scripture calling you to come into the light.
To confess.
To repent.
To receive forgiveness.
And to walk forward with Christ.
You may have already crossed a boundary.
But you do not have to keep crossing it.
You may have made choices you regret.
But regret does not have to become your identity.
You may have confused sexual excitement with spiritual intimacy.
But you can begin learning the difference.
And perhaps the person you intend to marry is waiting for you to have the courage to say what both of you have been afraid to admit.
"We need to do this differently."
Not because you love each other less.
But because you want to love each other better.
And perhaps, years from now, you will look back on this moment not as the night your relationship lost its excitement, but as the moment it began to grow in integrity.
The moment you stopped asking how close you could get to the edge.
And started asking how faithfully you could walk with Jesus.
The moment you realized that your relationship was never meant to become a private kingdom where your desires made the rules.
It was meant to become a place where Christ is honored.
Where truth can be spoken.
Where boundaries are respected.
Where repentance is possible.
Where forgiveness is practiced.
And where love learns to seek another person's good.
Because the greatest love story you will ever experience is not ultimately the story of two people standing at an altar.
It is the story of Jesus Christ giving Himself for sinners who could never save themselves.
Your fiancé may one day become your spouse.
But your spouse can never become your Savior.
Only Jesus can bear that place in your life.
And when He remains at the center, you are free to love another person without asking them to satisfy every longing of your soul.
So is sexting a sin if you're engaged and planning to marry?

If by sexting you mean deliberately exchanging sexually explicit messages or images for sexual arousal before marriage, the biblical principles concerning lust, sexual holiness, and self-control give Christians strong reason to reject that practice.
Engagement does not transform sexual conduct outside marriage into marital intimacy.
But the answer is not that every romantic message, every expression of attraction, or every honest conversation about future sexual intimacy is sinful.
Scripture calls us to discernment, not invented rules.
And it calls us to grace, not despair.
You do not honor marriage by pretending you are already married. You honor marriage by preparing to enter it faithfully.
And if you have failed, the invitation of Jesus is not to hide behind excuses or collapse beneath shame.
It is to come to Him.
Bring the hidden conversations.
Bring the compromised boundaries.
Bring the fear that you have disappointed God.
Bring the love you feel for your fiancé.
Bring the desire you don't always know how to manage.
Bring your whole heart into the light.
And ask Him to teach you how to love.
Not merely with words that ignite passion.
But with choices that reflect His character.
If you are engaged, dating, married, or hoping to marry someday, what do you believe is the hardest part of maintaining godly boundaries in a relationship?
Is it loneliness?
Fear of disappointing the person you love?
The pressure of modern dating culture?
The struggle to distinguish affection from lust?
Or the difficulty of admitting that a boundary has already been crossed?
You don't have to reveal private details or expose someone else's story.
But your honest answer may help another believer realize they are not alone in the struggle.
There is no shame in asking for prayer.
And there is no spiritual prize for pretending you never struggle.
Not as a weapon to use against someone else, but as a reminder to return to when your convictions begin to weaken.
You may have a friend quietly wrestling with this very question.
You may know an engaged couple who sincerely loves God but has never been taught how to think biblically about digital intimacy.
You may even know someone who has walked away from Christianity because the only message they ever heard about sexual sin was condemnation.
Because our mission is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
You glorify God first through faith in Christ and a life of love and obedience.
And one way you may freely choose to express that love is by helping make sound biblical teaching accessible to more people.
Those free resources matter.
Because someone who cannot afford a book still deserves access to biblical encouragement.
Someone struggling spiritually still deserves to encounter the Gospel.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry devoted to pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
And that's okay.
Prayer matters.
Sharing matters.
Faithful encouragement matters.
A sincere comment that helps someone feel less alone matters.
It is an invitation to surrender your life more fully to Jesus Christ.
Because one day the wedding photographs will fade.
The flowers will dry.
The excitement of the engagement season will become a memory.
And the phone that once held those late-night conversations will be replaced, forgotten, or thrown away.
But the choices you make in learning to love with honesty, patience, self-control, and faithfulness can shape the kind of person you become.
And if your story already includes failure, don't mistake that failure for the ending.
Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance.
His grace is still sufficient.
His truth is still good.
His forgiveness is still real.
And His power to transform a surrendered life has not diminished.
You may have sent messages you wish you could erase, but through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to write the final sentence of your future.
